question: A 35-year-old man is brought to his psychiatrist by his wife. The patient’s wife says his last visit was 3 years ago for an episode of depression. At that time, he was prescribed fluoxetine, which he did not take because he believed that his symptoms would subside on their own. A few months later, his wife says that he suddenly came out of his feelings of ‘depression’ and began to be more excitable and show pressured speech. She observed that he slept very little but had a heightened interest in sexual activity. This lasted for a few weeks, and he went back to his depressed state. He has continued to experience feelings of sadness and shows a lack of concentration at work. She often finds him crying, and he also expresses feelings of guilt for all the wrongs he allegedly did to her and to the family. There was a week where he had a brief time of excitability and was considering donating all their savings to a local charity. She is highly perturbed by his behavior and often finds it hard to predict what his mood will be like next. The patient denies any suicidal or homicidal ideations. A urine toxicology screen is negative. All laboratory tests, including thyroid hormone levels, are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "History of depression episode" -> "Prescribed fluoxetine" -> "Non-compliance with medication" -> "Sudden onset of excitability and pressured speech" -> "Decreased need for sleep" -> "Heightened interest in sexual activity" -> "Brief period of elevated mood" -> "Return to depressed state" -> "Feelings of sadness, guilt, lack of concentration" -> "Unpredictable mood swings" -> "Denies suicidal or homicidal ideations" -> "Negative urine toxicology screen" -> "Normal laboratory tests, including thyroid hormone levels" -> "Possible diagnosis of Bipolar disorder, type I" -> 80%

analysis: The patient's presentation is consistent with bipolar disorder, specifically bipolar disorder type II. He has a history of depressive episodes interspersed with hypomanic episodes, as evidenced by the periods of increased excitability, decreased need for sleep, heightened interest in sexual activity, and impulsivity such as considering donating all their savings to charity. The lack of full-blown mania and absence of psychotic symptoms suggest bipolar II rather than bipolar I.
